position: Refactor in place this year, but replace open-ended deferral with a hard, dated checkpoint (not a conditional 'if a concrete need emerges' trigger) at which the storage-format decision is forced, informed by instrumentation built into the refactor itself rather than a separate parallel pilot.

claims.text: A one-way door with zero roadmap slack raises the cost of a wrong bet under either path; it does not by itself favor refactor over rebuild, since a refactor that fails to change the slowness trajectory just spends the same scarce year arriving at the same irreversible choice under more pressure, not less.

Many three-year-old ingestion pipelines carry addressable bottlenecks (unindexed queries, serial processing, contention), but this is a base rate, not evidence about this system, so the refactor's expected payoff needs its own early instrumentation to confirm, not an assumption carried on the recommendation's back.

Rewrites of working systems commonly run longer than estimated and risk a second-system effect, arriving at the original's complexity before its reliability; none of the objections raised touched this claim, so it stands.

A rule of 'wait for a concrete near-term requirement before committing to streaming' never fires on its own, while deferral quietly raises the cost of the eventual cutover as more consumers, schemas, and operational habits calcify around the old format, so the decision needs a hard date, not a conditional trigger.

A resource-neutral 'parallel pilot' is incoherent under a genuine no-slack constraint, since it is itself a second concurrent workstream requiring streaming expertise and dual infrastructure, and even a real pilot would undersample the failure modes that only appear at production scale (skew, compaction, retention, access-pattern shift); so the storage-format decision should be informed by lightweight instrumentation added during the refactor, not a separate pilot.

assumptions: The slowness is primarily a throughput/latency problem rather than a correctness or data-model problem that refactoring cannot fix.
The team has not already validated the streaming storage format against production-scale data.
No external commitment (contract, compliance deadline, customer SLA) forces streaming this year regardless of risk.

The org has capacity for one workstream (the refactor) this year, not for a refactor plus a concurrent streaming pilot; that lack of spare capacity is the same constraint the position is built on, so the plan cannot quietly assume it away.
would_change_my_mind: Evidence that the current pipeline's slowness stems from an architectural ceiling that no in-place refactor can plausibly reach.
A concrete, already-committed downstream dependency (customer contract, regulatory deadline) requiring streaming semantics within the year.
Data showing in-place refactor attempts on this codebase have historically failed or produced negligible gains, making refactor the actually-risky option.

Evidence that lightweight instrumentation added during the refactor cannot capture the failure modes needed to validate a storage format before the checkpoint date, which would make the forcing function meaningless and remove the main reason to prefer refactor-then-decide over rebuild-now.
Evidence the team has already built and battle-tested comparable streaming pipelines before, reducing execution risk on the rebuild.
nuance: The crux moved from 'can a pilot de-risk the storage-format bet' to 'can a forcing function survive the temptation to defer again.'
